extracted.subtask_description: Procedure and factors for determining patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101 for claims that recite or involve laws of nature, natural phenomena, natural principles, and/or natural products. Includes a three-question flowchart, a factor-based 'significantly different' analysis, examples, and a form rejection paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall three-question subject matter eligibility process
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining what applicant invented and establishing the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim (per MPEP §2103), walk through three questions in sequence to determine whether the claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter; if not, the claim is prima facie ineligible and should be rejected using revised form paragraph 7.05.13.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 1: statutory category. Question 2: does the claim recite or involve one or more judicial exceptions? Question 3: does the claim as a whole recite something significantly different than the judicial exception(s)? If at any point the answer dictates ineligibility, use form paragraph 7.05.13 and precede with form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05. For claims reciting abstract ideas continue to use MPEP §2106(II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question 1 — Statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the claimed invention directed to one of the four statutory patent-eligible subject matter categories: process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP §706.03 for form paragraphs). If yes, proceed to Question 2. Note: claims to humans per se are not directed to a statutory subject matter category (Section 33(a) AIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question 2 — Judicial exception identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim recite or involve one or more judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural principles, natural phenomena, natural products)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no, the claim is patent-eligible and analysis is complete. If yes or unclear, proceed to Question 3. Examples of natural products include chemicals derived from natural sources, foods, metals, minerals, natural materials, nucleic acids, organisms, proteins/peptides, and other substances found in or derived from nature. If any doubt whether the claim recites a judicial exception, treat it as requiring further analysis under Question 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question 3 — 'Significantly different' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claim as a whole recite something significantly different than the judicial exception(s)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For abstract idea claims, analyze using only MPEP §2106(II). For other judicial exceptions use the factor-based 'significantly different' analysis set forth in Part II. If the claim as a whole is not significantly different, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 using revised form paragraph 7.05.13; if it is significantly different, the claim is patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / examples of judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions include abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural principles, natural phenomena, and natural products. These exceptions reflect the judicial view that fundamental tools of scientific and technological work are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also note other terms have been used (natural phenomena, products of nature, naturally occurring things, scientific principles, mental processes, mathematical algorithms/formulas). When a claim recites something similar to a natural product, proceed to the 'significantly different' analysis regardless of claim language like 'isolated', 'recombinant', or 'synthetic'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor-based analysis for 'significantly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites or involves a judicial exception other than an abstract idea, determine whether the claim as a whole is significantly different from the judicial exception by weighing multiple factors (a through l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A significant difference can be shown by (1) elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception that practically apply it in a significant way (add significantly more), and/or (2) features or steps that demonstrate the claimed subject matter is markedly different from what exists in nature. Not every factor will be relevant to every claim; consider and weigh all relevant factors and evidence. On balance, if the totality of relevant factors weigh toward eligibility, the claim qualifies; if against, it should be rejected. The weight accorded each factor varies with the facts (analogous to Wands analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor a) — Product claim markedly different in structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that initially appears to be a natural product, but after analysis is determined to be non-naturally occurring and markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate, identify differences between the recited product and naturally occurring products and assess whether differences together rise to the level of a marked difference in structure. A marked difference must be significant (more than incidental/trivial). Routine or conventional human manipulation that produced the marked difference does not prevent it from weighing in favor of eligibility (e.g., cDNA, hybrid plants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor b) — Elements/steps that impose meaningful limits on claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that impose meaningful limits on claim scope, i.e., the elements/steps narrow the scope so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: specific dosage and treatment period in a medical treatment claim that prevent broad foreclosure of other uses. If satisfied, this factor weighs toward eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor c) — Elements/steps significantly related to the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that relate to the judicial exception in a significant way — more than nominally, insignificantly, or tangentially related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: steps that manipulate, integrate, or materially interact with the natural product/principle (e.g., positioning and filtering light; manipulating a protein with a specific antibody). If satisfied, this factor weighs toward eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor d) — More than general instructions to apply the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that do more than describe the judicial exception(s) with general instructions to apply or use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that contain only high-level directives to 'apply' or 'use' a natural principle are less likely to qualify. Specific, particularized steps (dosage, times, filtering/positioning) satisfying this factor weigh toward eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor e) — Particular machine or transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that include a particular machine or transformation of a particular article, where the machine/transformation implements or integrates the judicial exception(s) into a particular practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2106(II)(B)(1) for explanation of machine-or-transformation considerations. Satisfying this factor supports eligibility; lack of a machine/transformation does not by itself make a claim ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor f) — Features more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites one or more elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that add a feature that is more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements are novel in the relevant art or not routine/conventional for the claimed application, this factor weighs toward eligibility. Conversely, if the additional elements are well-known and routine in the field, this factor does not favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor g) — Product claim not markedly different (weighs against eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim is a product claim reciting something that appears to be a natural product that is not markedly different in structure from naturally occurring products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recited product is structurally indistinguishable in any meaningful way from what exists in nature (e.g., purified compound with same structure), factor g) weighs against eligibility. Mere isolation that changes bonds (e.g., isolated gene fragment) may not be a marked difference per Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor h) — Additional elements recited at a high level of generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) at a high level of generality such that substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception(s) are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level recitations that effectively preempt substantial practical uses of the judicial exception weigh against eligibility. Specific limitations that narrow applications avoid this problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor i) — Additional elements are required to apply the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that must be used/taken by others to apply the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim requires steps or elements that everyone must perform to practice the natural principle (thereby foreclosing others), this factor weighs against eligibility. If alternatives are available (different antibodies, methods), this factor may not be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor j) — Additional elements are well-understood, purely conventional or routine (weighs against eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are well-understood, purely conventional or routine in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the supposedly limiting steps are routine and conventional, they do not add significantly more to the judicial exception and thus weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor k) — Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that are insignificant extra-solution activity, e.g., are merely appended to the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional steps merely amount to post-solution activity or insignificant appendages, they do not make the claim significantly different and weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor l) — Mere field of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recites elements/steps in addition to the judicial exception(s) that amount to nothing more than a mere field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting a judicial exception to a field of use (e.g., use of sunlight only for mood disorders) without more does not render claim eligible; such limitations weigh against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing factors and totality approach
rubrics_metrics.description: On balance, the relevant factors should be weighed together; if the totality of relevant factors weighs toward eligibility the claim is eligible, if against, it should be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must carefully consider every relevant factor and related evidence before concluding. Not every factor is relevant to every claim; the weight accorded each factor varies with the facts. This factor-based analysis is similar to the Wands undue experimentation analysis (see MPEP 2164.01(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with other statutes and compact prosecution guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: §101 is not the sole tool for determining patentability; where a claim encompasses a judicial exception such as a natural product, sections 102, 103, and 112 provide additional tools for ensuring the claim meets patentability conditions. Under compact prosecution, Office personnel should state all non-cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obviousness (103), novelty (102), and written description/enablement (112) rejections as appropriate in addition to §101. Ensure initial Office action is comprehensive as to non-cumulative grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation prerequisite (MPEP §2103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before performing the three-question analysis, determine what the applicant invented and establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in accordance with MPEP §2103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate claim construction is a prerequisite to applying the eligibility questions and factor analysis; examination record and specification should be consulted to understand the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea claims — continue to follow MPEP §2106(II)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no change to examination of claims reciting an abstract idea; such claims should continue to be analyzed for subject matter eligibility using existing guidance in MPEP §2106(II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim recites both an abstract idea and another judicial exception (e.g., a natural product), the analysis in MPEP §2106(II) controls eligibility for abstract-idea recitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.05.13 usage and explanatory content
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised form paragraph 7.05.13 should be used when rejecting claims that recite or involve a law of nature/natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product for lack of subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101. It must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracket 2 of the form must identify the judicial exception(s) recited and explain why the claim features do not result in the claim as a whole reciting something significantly different. Explain why features do not add significantly more and/or do not demonstrate a marked difference from nature; e.g., show additional elements are extra-solution activity, mere field of use, or well-understood/purely conventional/routine. The explanation must be sufficient to establish a prima facie case of patent ineligibility under §101.
